brief.ask: Set the art direction for 12 boys' birthday evites (dinosaurs, space, trucks, soccer, pirates, heroes, robots, sharks, safari, knights, race cars, ninjas). Each one has a 15-second tap game or scratch-and-reveal before the details. Say what makes a parent forward this instead of a text.
brief.audience: Parents of 3 to 10 year olds sending to other parents; the kids play the game on a parent's phone.
brief.feeling: Wonder and momentum, a toy brought to life, never cheap or loud for its own sake.
constraints: Surface: Plajah Evites, an invitation opened on a phone browser by guests who never sign up; also shared as a link preview and QR.

Build method (fixed): each design is a layered Tela document: a generated art plate, separate transparent foreground cut-outs that drift and react to phone tilt, a WebGL effects layer (foil shimmer, light leaks, bokeh, particles, candle flicker) revealed through masks, and live text in Tela. Names, dates and venues are never baked into the art.
Bar: consumer-facing, jaw-dropping, high-end professional. Must stay legible at 390px wide, honour reduced motion, and load fast on mobile data.
No copyrighted characters; kids art is original or Plajah-owned.
references: Exploration grid A: collectible-toy 3D dinosaurs in a golden-hour jungle with a glowing volcano and balloons; warm, film-grade; empty dirt foreground for type.
Exploration grid B: painterly nebula space scenes, a small rocket past a ringed planet and a smiling moon; deep blue starfield bottom third for type.

proposals.title: The Illuminated Bestiary Evite
proposals.idea: Each theme is a hand-measured page from a master codex — a medieval bestiary or astronomical atlas redrawn for the subject — so the invitation arrives with the weight of a found artifact and the game is an act of revelation, not distraction.
proposals.geometry: A strict golden-section rectangle governs the full 390px canvas: the art plate occupies the major rectangle (upper ~60.8%), the type zone the minor rectangle below. Within the art plate, a 6-column, 4-row harmonic grid (derived from the same ratio) positions every foreground cut-out at a named interval — no element floats arbitrarily. The game layer sits at the exact optical center of the major rectangle, so the tap or scratch resolves the composition rather than interrupting it. Borders are ruled at 1/12 of canvas width, echoing the gutter proportion of a Bodoni folio.
proposals.typography: Primary wordmark and theme title: Cormorant Garamond Italic Display, tracked −10, set at a scale that makes the ascenders touch the ruled border — the cap-height IS the measure. Guest-facing details: Cormorant Garamond Regular, 16px, generous leading (1.6×) for phone legibility. Game prompt line: Freight Text Pro Italic, slightly smaller, set in a hairline-ruled cartouche. All type live in Tela, never baked. Small caps used for date/time to maintain hierarchy without shouting. Zero decorative fonts; the serif does all dramatic work through size contrast alone.
proposals.imageLogic: No photographs. Each art plate is an original Plajah illustration built to resemble a hand-painted atlas or natural-history plate: opaque gouache-style rendering with visible dry-brush edges, ink outline at variable weight (heavier at silhouette, broken mid-form), and a vellum-tone ground that reads warm under the foil shimmer layer. The dinosaur becomes a Cuvierian reconstruction; the rocket becomes an Orrery diagram; the shark becomes a Gesner woodcut redrawn with volume. These are not vintage pastiches — the forms are bold and legible at small size — but the image logic is taxonomic clarity, not photorealism or cartoon.
proposals.texture: The art plate sits on a simulated vellum ground: a photographed sheet of hot-press watercolor paper (Plajah-owned material scan, 2048px) is used as the base texture layer, multiplied at 30% opacity beneath the illustration. The ruled border is a thin foil-shimmer line revealed through the WebGL mask — at rest it reads as a gold ink rule; on load it catches a single light leak travelling left to right in 1.2 seconds, then stills. Foreground cut-outs (e.g., a pterodactyl wing, a planet ring, a knight's gauntlet) have a slight paper-grain edge rather than a clean vector clip, achieved by a noise-displacement mask in Tela.
proposals.motion: Sequence is strict and earns each beat: (1) On open, a 0.8s fade brings the vellum ground and illustration to full opacity — no bounce, no overshoot, a page turning. (2) A single light leak crosses the gold border rule left-to-right (1.2s, ease-in-out), then extinguishes; this is the only unsolicited motion. (3) Foreground cut-outs respond to phone tilt via gyroscope parallax: the nearest layer (e.g., the pterodactyl) drifts at ±8px, the mid layer at ±4px, the background plate at ±2px — governed by a linear spring constant so the drift has weight, not jitter. (4) The game zone pulses once with a soft bokeh particle bloom (1s, then idle) to invite interaction. (5) Game resolution — tap to hatch the egg, scratch to reveal the planet — triggers a foil-shimmer burst radiating from the center outward to the border rule, settling in 0.6s. (6) Details text fades in from 0 at the conclusion of t
proposals.productionMethod: Illustration produced in Procreate on iPad Pro using a custom dry-brush/ink-outline brush set; exported as layered PSD with named groups (ground, mid, foreground-cutout-1, foreground-cutout-2, game-zone). Tela ingests layers as separate assets; the paper-scan texture is a Plajah-licensed material photograph. WebGL effects (foil shimmer, light leak, bokeh bloom) are written as Tela shader passes keyed to named mask layers — the border rule shimmer is a single-pass directional gradient shader. Gyroscope parallax is a Tela motion component with configurable spring constant and dead-zone for reduced-motion compliance. Game mechanic (tap-to-hatch or scratch-to-reveal) is a Tela interaction layer: scratch uses pointer-events to erase a top mask revealing the illustration beneath; tap-to-hatch plays a 12-frame sprite animation of a cracking egg or equivalent object, also Plajah-owned. Live text
proposals.humanTrace: The dry-brush ink edge of every silhouette — the place where the bristles splay and the line breaks — is preserved from the original Procreate stroke and is visible at 390px. It is the mark that tells a parent this was drawn, not generated. The paper-scan ground carries the actual grain of a specific sheet. These two traces together give the artifact quality that makes a parent stop scrolling and hand the phone to the child.
proposals.risk: The codex register may read as adult or precious to parents expecting loud primary-color energy, and the restrained motion may feel underbuilt beside competitors. The risk is worth taking because it is the only direction that gives the child something that feels genuinely rare — a found object, not a product — and rarity is exactly what makes a parent forward a link instead of sending a text. A parent forwards what they are proud to have found.

I will hold that the foil burst radiating to the border rule and then settling is the correct resolution precisely because it completes the geometry rather than overwhelming it. proposals.title: Inked, Torn, Then Sent
proposals.idea: Each evite begins as a hand-pulled linocut or woodblock print — physically carved, inked, pressed onto kraft or newsprint, then photographed under raking light so every gouge and roller streak is visible — and the digital layer acts as a varnish over that physical dent, not a replacement for it.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 390px wide; the art plate is a full-bleed photograph of the actual printed sheet, with deckled or torn bottom edge where type lives on a raw paper strip — no clean crop, no rounded card corners; foreground cut-outs float above the plate as if peeled off the same print run; the scratch-or-tap zone is a rectangular ink-block in the upper two-thirds, deliberately off-center by 7–12px to signal handmade register error
proposals.typography: Headings in Playfair Display Black at large scale, letterspaced tight, set in a single warm off-white so it reads like debossed foil on the print; event details in IBM Plex Mono Regular at 14px, left-aligned on the torn paper strip — monospace because it looks like a typed label stapled to the print; NO display typeface that imitates brushwork — that is decoration pretending to be process
proposals.imageLogic: No stock photography. Each theme begins with a real carved block: dinosaurs get a lino rex with hatching scratches; space gets a woodblock planet with radial gouge lines; trucks get a relief print with tread-pattern rollers pressed unevenly across the block. The block is inked, pressed, photographed on a lightbox at 45-degree raking angle so every ridge casts a shadow. That photograph is the art plate. Foreground cut-outs are photographed separately — painted paper animals, foil-wrapped rocket, folded paper knight helmet — then masked and layered. The WebGL foil shimmer is masked to only the ink-heavy ridges, proving the wood was carved before the screen touched it.
proposals.texture: Actual ink on newsprint or kraft, photographed. Roller streaks are preserved. Ink squash at block edges is preserved. The torn paper strip at the bottom is torn by hand on set and photographed. No digital paper texture filters — those are decoration. If a texture cannot be pointed to in the making photograph, it is cut.
proposals.motion: On load: the art-plate photograph fades up in 0.4s, no easing flourish. Foreground cut-outs drift in response to phone tilt at low parallax depth — they move because the phone moves, not on a timer, so the child controls it. The scratch-or-tap game: a layer of printed black ink (photographed, same block) sits over the reveal; the child's finger path removes it in real time, exposing the WebGL foil shimmer underneath — the shimmer only where the finger has passed, rewarding slow deliberate scratching over frantic tapping. After 15 seconds or full reveal: the torn paper strip slides up from bottom at 0.6s, details appear in Plex Mono. Reduced-motion mode: tilt disabled, scratch layer pre-revealed at 60% opacity, strip already in position.
proposals.productionMethod: Physical production first: carve 12 blocks (one per theme), one ink color per block plus a second pass in gold or red for accent. Photograph each print on a lightbox. Photograph foreground props — folded paper, painted cardboard, foil-wrapped objects — against neutral ground. Bring both into Tela as the art plate and foreground cut-out layers. Write WebGL mask logic so shimmer clips to the photographed ink ridges. Build scratch-reveal in canvas, finger path stored as a bezier that expands 18px radius per touch point. Names, dates, venue live in Tela text layer, never baked. QR and link preview use a single representative frame of the art plate — the torn edge is visible in the preview thumbnail, which is the whole argument for opening it.
proposals.humanTrace: The gouge marks in each block are visible in the art plate photograph under raking light. Roller streaks cross the plate in one direction. Ink squash at block edge is present. The torn paper strip bottom edge is irregular and photographable. These are not simulated — they are documented in a making photograph that exists before any screen is opened.
proposals.risk: Parents expecting bright vector illustration or photorealistic 3D will see something that looks, for one second, rough. That one second of doubt is the point — it resolves into recognition that someone physically made this, which is the reason a parent forwards it instead of a text. The risk is that a client mistakes evidence of making for evidence of low budget. That risk is worth it because the alternative — smooth, frictionless, forgettable — is what every other evite platform already does. The photocopied-four-times test: the ink ridges survive. The gouge lines survive. The torn edge survives. The WebGL shimmer does not survive, and that is correct — the shimmer was never the thing.

arguesWith.why: The Futurist will argue that beginning with a physical carved block and photographing it is an inefficient bottleneck — that a generative system can produce equivalent texture variation faster and at scale. proposals.title: State Machines Wearing Birthday Hats
proposals.idea: Each evite is a miniature physics engine disguised as a party invitation — the theme is the input variable, the child's tap or tilt is the state change, and the reveal is the system behaving correctly, not performing magic.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 390×844px viewport treated as a sensor field, not a canvas. A strict 12-column baseline grid anchors live text in the bottom 220px; above that, the art plate is a full-bleed simulation space divided into three depth planes — background (parallax coefficient 0.15), midground cut-outs (coefficient 0.45), foreground particles (coefficient 1.0). No decorative borders. Proportional rule: the game interaction zone occupies exactly the golden ratio cut of the screen height (top 521px). The reveal boundary is a hard physics edge, not a fade.
proposals.typography: Clash Display (Variable, weight 400–700) for the party headline — its geometric grotesque skeleton reads as designed-object, not playful-font-store. Numerals and dates in Tabular figures, tracked +20, so names and times sit on the grid like instrument readouts. Theme name runs large (72–88px, uppercase, weight 600) flush left. Secondary info in Fragment Mono 13px — signals that the system knows what it is. No hand-lettered scripts; the fun comes from the physics, not the typeface performing enthusiasm.
proposals.imageLogic: No photography. Each art plate is a computed 3D render: Blender Cycles, HDRI-lit, physically based materials, exported as a 1440×3120px static plate at 2× density then compressed to WebP at quality 82. The render is not illustration-style; it is object-photography-style — depth of field, subsurface scatter on organic forms, real shadow termination. Dinosaurs have scute micro-texture from a scanned reptile skin tile. Spaceship panels show tooling marks from a photographed aluminium offcut used as a normal-map source. Trucks have painted-metal flake in the base coat. Every theme's 3D scene is lit from a single motivated source so the WebGL foil layer's light direction matches the render — dimensional coherence is non-negotiable. The generated art plate is the physical world; the WebGL layer is the physics response.
proposals.texture: Two-layer texture contract: (1) the art plate carries photographic surface — scanned dirt for safari and knights, brushed titanium for robots, carbon-fibre weave for race cars, wet neoprene for sharks — applied as a roughness/normal overlay in the render, not as a Photoshop filter; (2) the WebGL effects layer adds zero fake texture. Its job is light behaviour only: foil shimmer responds to real deviceorientation API data (the shimmer highlight moves as the phone tilts, 60fps, capped at 12fps under reduced-motion preference with a stepped interpolation so it still reads as responsive). Bokeh particles are billboarded sprites with a physically correct hexagonal aperture shape per theme's implied lens (long telephoto for safari, wide for space).
proposals.motion: Sequence is a state machine with four named states. STATE 0 — Load: art plate fades in at 280ms, foreground cut-outs drop from +40px at 380ms staggered 60ms apart, particle layer initialises at opacity 0. STATE 1 — Idle: gyro-tilt drives foreground parallax continuously; foil shimmer tracks orientation; particles drift at 0.4px/frame. No looping animation; the phone IS the animation input. STATE 2 — Game (15 seconds): tap-to-reveal or scratch gesture activates. Dinosaur: tap each egg, it cracks open on a spring physics curve (tension 180, damping 12) releasing a hatchling that settles with a secondary wobble — the wobble duration is computed from the device's touch velocity so a hard tap gives a fast wobble, a soft tap gives a slow one. Space: tilt the phone to steer the rocket through an asteroid field, asteroids are rigid-body circles, collisions resolve with impulse response. Trucks:
proposals.productionMethod: Blender 3D renders (one per theme, one artist per scene, credited internally) → WebP export → Tela art plate layer. Foreground cut-outs are separate PNG-alpha exports from the same Blender scene, ensuring lighting coherence. WebGL effects layer written in raw GLSL with deviceorientation API binding — no Three.js overhead, hand-authored shaders so the load budget stays under 180kb for the effects layer. Game logic per theme is a standalone ES module (~12–18kb gzipped) with a shared physics micro-library (custom spring integrator, ~4kb). Live text layer is Tela's native text engine, never baked. Total target load: art plate 120–160kb, cut-outs 30–50kb total, shaders + game logic 30kb, fonts subset 22kb. QR and link-preview use a static frame extracted from STATE 0 end-position, no animation dependency.
proposals.humanTrace: Every 3D render uses at least one photographed physical material as a source asset: the dinosaur skin roughness map is a macro photograph of a Nile monitor lizard scale tile shot in-house under raking light; the space nebula background uses a long-exposure photograph of smoke in backlight composited into the HDRI; the shark scene's water-surface normal map is a video frame of a water tank shot at 240fps and frozen. The game interactions record the child's actual gesture path — scratch direction, tap force via touch event pressure where available — and replay it as a ghost trace in STATE 3 for two seconds, so the parent sees exactly what their kid did. That trace is the child's handwriting inside the machine.
proposals.risk: The system-first approach risks feeling cold if the 3D renders do not carry enough warmth and material specificity — a physically correct robot is still a robot, and a three-year-old needs to feel delight before understanding physics. The bet is that correct light behaviour (shadow direction matching foil shimmer direction, spring physics that respond to touch force) produces a felt quality of realness that children and parents register emotionally without naming it. If the renders are underlit or the physics constants are wrong, the whole premise collapses into an expensive tech demo. The risk is worth it because the alternative — illustrated characters with particle confetti — is already the ceiling of the category, and this brief explicitly asks for a toy brought to life, which means behaviour, not decoration.

arguesWith.why: The Baroque Dramatist will want a reveal moment — a curtain pull, a crescendo, a single spectacular transition that the parent screenshots. I am arguing that the reveal is not a moment, it is a state reached through the child's own input, and its quality is proportional to the quality of the physics, not the drama of the transition. proposals.title: Field-Documented Wonders, Hand-Verified
proposals.idea: Each evite is a field naturalist's specimen page — a photographed physical diorama built from painted paper, carved balsa, and dyed fabric, documented under raking light, then animated so the cut-out layers drift with phone tilt as if the box lid has just been lifted.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 9:19.5 phone canvas divided into three unequal horizontal registers: top 55% is the specimen-box diorama photograph with a ragged torn-paper lower edge; middle 30% is a cream-tinted field-notebook ruled zone holding all live text; bottom 15% is the game zone — a full-bleed scratch panel or tap target. No grid symmetry; the diorama is photographed slightly off-axis (3–5° cant) to read as a real object on a desk, not a centred poster.
proposals.typography: Headings: Canela Deck Regular (serif with naturalist warmth, generous ink traps) set at 32–38px, mixed case, loose tracking 0.02em. Child's name hand-lettered on a physical paper strip photographed and composited — never baked into the art plate, but placed as a live Tela text layer using a single consistent handwriting variable font (Caveat) so it reads as written on the label after personalisation. Detail text: iA Writer Quattro at 13px, uppercase labels with 0.12em tracking mimicking specimen annotation. All type lives in the ruled notebook register, never over the diorama image.
proposals.imageLogic: Physical dioramas are constructed in-studio for all 12 themes — e.g., Dinosaurs: carved balsa Brachiosaurus painted with gouache and sealed, placed in a box lined with dyed-green tissue-paper foliage and orange crepe-paper sky; Space: black velvet box interior, hand-rolled aluminium-foil planet with fabric Saturn ring, small painted balsa rocket. Each box is photographed under a single raking tungsten source (warm, directional, casting real shadows) on a medium-format mirrorless body. Foreground cut-out layers — a leaf, a cloud, a shark fin — are photographed separately on white, masked, and placed as tilt-reactive Tela foreground planes. WebGL foil shimmer is gated entirely by the physical paint-chip topography of each carved model, honouring the maker's hand. No stock photography; no AI-generated imagery.
proposals.texture: Physical paper, balsa, fabric, gouache, and crepe are the primary surfaces. The notebook zone uses a photographed cream Fabriano page scan as a texture overlay at 40% opacity so ruled lines and paper tooth read through the live type. The scratch-and-reveal game panel is a photographed sheet of crumpled kitchen foil over coloured card — the digital scratch mask follows the actual foil crinkle topology, so scratching feels materially honest.
proposals.motion: Sequence on open: 0–0.4s the diorama photograph fades in from black as if a box lid lifts (parallax: background layer moves 2px up, foreground cut-outs 8px up). 0.4–1.2s: one key floating element (balloon, asteroid, shark fin) drifts in from the torn-paper edge with a gentle ease-in-out, settling to a slow idle float on gyroscope tilt. 1.2–3s: the foil shimmer on the diorama's painted surfaces pulses once, warm-to-cool, gated by the physical paint-chip mask. Game zone: the foil-crinkle scratch panel sits inert with a subtle shimmer pulse every 4s until touched; on scratch/tap the card colour beneath is revealed in a radial wipe that follows the actual crinkle paths. Reduced-motion mode: no float, no shimmer pulse; the diorama is static; scratch reveal is an instant crossfade.
proposals.productionMethod: 12 physical dioramas constructed by a single prop stylist working in a fixed studio setup across two shoot days (one light position maintained for visual consistency across themes). Medium-format RAW files retouched for colour consistency, then layered in Tela: background plate, mid-cut-outs, foreground cut-outs, WebGL mask derived from a greyscale height map baked from the physical model's photogrammetry scan. Notebook text zone is a Tela live-text region; child's name, date, venue pull from the invitation data fields. Game mechanic: scratch panel is a canvas element with pointer-events tracking touch paths against the foil-crinkle topology PNG; reveal threshold at 60% area scratched. QR and link-preview thumbnail is a flat crop of the diorama photograph at 1200×630px with the theme name in Canela Deck overlaid — no game UI, loads instantly.
proposals.humanTrace: The raking tungsten shadows on carved balsa and the paint-chip topography of each hand-gouached model are permanently visible in the photograph and determine every shimmer and parallax path in the digital layer. A parent can see the brush strokes. The child's name appears in Caveat as if written on the specimen label with a felt-tip pen. The scratch panel crinkles are real foil geometry, not procedural noise.
proposals.risk: The physical production cost (two shoot days, prop stylist, 12 dioramas) is real and front-loaded. The risk is worth it because it produces genuinely unrepeatable images that read as precious objects — the reason a parent forwards this instead of a text is that the evite looks like something someone *made*, not something someone *rendered*. Parents in the 3–10 age bracket are primed to value visible craft because they spend their days doing it with their children.

arguesWith.why: The Futurist will propose procedurally generated creature variants, GPU-rendered volumetric jungles, and real-time physics — all of which are technically impressive and load fast but erase the maker's hand entirely. proposals.title: Miniature Opera Houses, All Twelve
proposals.idea: Each evite is a lit stage: a curtain of physical darkness parts on a diorama world at the exact moment the child taps, so the game IS the reveal and the reveal IS the invitation.
proposals.geometry: Portrait 390px wide, divided into three unequal acts — a compressed dark proscenium header (roughly 18% of screen height) that collapses downward as the game resolves, a sovereign central stage plate (60%) where the world lives at forced-perspective depth, and a shallow footlight shelf (22%) in deep shadow holding live type. No grid of equal columns. The asymmetry is architectural: the eye is told where the drama lives before a single pixel loads.
proposals.typography: Display headlines in Freight Display Pro Italic — Renaissance warmth, optical weight that reads as carved rather than printed, set at 52–64px tracking tightly so letters feel pressed together like relief lettering on a theatre marquee. Supporting details in Söhne Mono at 11px for date and venue — its mechanical evenness reads as a playbill's fine print without irony. Case is mixed: the theme word in full caps, the child's name in title case at 1.4× the theme word's size, because the name is always the star. Never sentence case on a birthday.
proposals.imageLogic: No photography. Each world is a constructed physical maquette — dinosaurs: 3D-printed resin figures painted with Vallejo acrylics and photographed under a single tungsten practical with a DIY foil bounce card to simulate golden-hour fill; space: vacuum-formed styrene planets suspended on monofilament against stretched black velvet, lit with a fiber-optic point source; trucks, knights, race cars: balsa and cardstock models with applied tissue-paper weathering. Each maquette is photographed at macro depth-of-field so foreground elements go into extreme bokeh while the mid-ground hero object is tack-sharp — this is the chiaroscuro, built in the lens not in post. Images are then separated into three parallax layers: deep background (blurred, slow drift on tilt), hero object (sharp, medium drift), and practical-light practical — candle, torch, headlight — isolated as its own foreground layer
proposals.texture: The stage-plate background carries a subtle grain baked at the photography stage — real film-grain from shooting on a Canon 5D with a vintage 50mm f/1.4 at ISO 800. The proscenium header is a WebGL-rendered velvet-weave mask: the shimmer catches tilt as foil does, but its pattern is a scanned piece of actual embossed theatrical curtain fabric (Plajah-owned scan). The footlight shelf is matte near-black with a 2px hot-white ruled line separating it from the stage — this line is the single brightest element on screen before the reveal, drawing the eye downward to where the name will appear.
proposals.motion: Act I (0–0.4s on load): the proscenium header drops from the top, not fading — a mechanical drop, 12fps stepped easing, each step a discrete position, no interpolation between them. This is the wooden-toy hesitation I now believe in. Act II (tap/scratch game, 0–15s): the game mechanic is theme-specific — dinosaurs: tap erupting volcano sparks that scatter across the stage plate; space: drag a comet trail to 'charge' the rocket; trucks: tilt phone to back a truck into a loading bay; soccer: flick a ball into goal — but all twelve share the same reveal architecture: as the game resolves, the proscenium header collapses fully downward (again stepped, 12fps) and the deep background brightens from near-black to golden/chromatic key light in 0.8 seconds — a sunrise, not a fade. proposals.productionMethod: Twelve physical maquettes built by a prop fabricator working from Plajah-supplied theme briefs. Each maquette photographed in a light-controlled studio space — one shooting day per four themes, three themes per half-day. RAW files separated in Photoshop into depth layers, exported as WebP at 85% quality. Tela document structure: layer 1 background WebP (blurred, slow), layer 2 hero WebP (sharp), layer 3 practical-light PNG sequence (6-frame loop for flicker, 12fps), layer 4 WebGL mask (velvet curtain, foil shimmer, bokeh particles keyed to game completion percentage), layer 5 live Tela text block. Game logic is a Tela interaction module — theme-specific input type, shared completion event that fires the sunrise. Names, dates, venues injected as Tela variables, never touching the art layers.
proposals.humanTrace: The maquette construction is the trace. Visible brushstroke edges on painted resin dinosaur scales. A slight lean in the monofilament planet suspension — not corrected in post, because the imperfection is the proof of weight. The scanned embossed curtain fabric carries a pressed crease from where the fabric was folded in storage. These are not mistakes to fix; they are the evidence that a hand was here, and they are what make a parent stop scrolling.
proposals.risk: Parents may not immediately recognize 'dark proscenium opening' as an invitation — the first half-second reads as a broken load or a black screen. This risk is worth taking because the alternative (a bright, immediately legible card) is every other digital invitation ever sent. The dark opening IS the promise: something is about to be revealed. If the stepped curtain drop fires cleanly in 0.4 seconds, the parent understands. The interaction window to lose them is narrow; the reward for keeping them is that they have never seen a birthday evite behave this way, and that is why they forward it.

proposals.title: One Signal. Nothing Else.
proposals.idea: Each evite is a single, silent object — one creature or machine held in precise negative space — that becomes legible only when the child touches it, earning the information through restraint, not spectacle.
proposals.geometry: 390px fixed column. A single centered subject occupies exactly 61.8% of viewport height — the golden section used structurally, not decoratively. Above and below: pure void. No border, no frame, no background fill except the subject's own ambient light spill. The scratch or tap game lives entirely within the subject silhouette — the dinosaur's flank, the rocket's hull, the shark's jaw — so the mechanic and the image are the same object, never layered on top. Text enters only after the game resolves: name, date, venue in a single left-aligned column, 16px baseline grid, 56px from the bottom edge. Nothing else occupies the canvas.
proposals.typography: Söhne Mono for all live text — name, date, venue. Tracked at +80 for dates and venues; name set at 28px, all-caps, no weight change. Zero decorative type. Zero theme fonts. The restraint of the typeface is the contrast against the 3D subject — that gap is where the personality lives. Reduced-motion fallback: type is already present, static, same position.
proposals.imageLogic: Each subject is a Plajah-original 3D render: hyperreal surface detail — scales, rivets, chain mail, fur — but photographed lighting, not studio CG. A single directional light source, raked at 15 degrees, casts one hard shadow onto the void ground plane. That shadow is the only evidence the subject exists in space. No background environment. No jungle, no nebula, no ocean floor. The subject floats; the shadow anchors it. This is the direct argument against Exploration Grid A and B: the environment is not the idea — the creature is.
proposals.texture: The subject surface carries all tactile weight: the dinosaur's scales are displacement-mapped from a scan of actual lizard skin; the robot's chassis from photographed brushed aluminium; the shark's hide from a macro photograph of shagreen leather. The void background is not white — it is a photographed sheet of 300gsm uncoated stock, slightly warm, slightly fibrous, visible only in the WebGL layer as a 4% grain. Organic texture bound to a mechanical constraint: the grain exists only within a 12-frame tilt cycle — it shifts with phone orientation, making the void feel physical without decorating it.
proposals.motion: Tilt reaction first — the subject drifts 8px maximum on x and y axes, shadow stretches proportionally, one foil-shimmer pass moves across the surface material at tilt angle. This happens before any tap. The 15-second game: the child's finger scratches or taps within the silhouette boundary; a WebGL mask erodes the surface, revealing the party details printed on the inside of the creature — as if the dinosaur were hollow and the invitation was always inside it. Details emerge from within the subject, not beneath it. After reveal: the subject settles, the shadow sharpens, the type locks. No loop, no idle animation. The object rests.
proposals.productionMethod: 3D renders produced in Cinema 4D with physical renderer; single HDRI light from a photographed overcast sky file — no synthetic lighting rigs. Shadow baked as a separate transparent PNG layer. Grain overlay is a photographed paper scan, tiled and composited in the WebGL layer at 4% opacity. Scratch mechanic built in WebGL using a displacement mask driven by pointer events; the mask shape is the subject's alpha channel, so the erasure is always contained within the silhouette. Tela receives: art plate (subject render), shadow layer, grain layer, WebGL mask definition, live text fields. Names and dates are never in the art plate.
proposals.humanTrace: The shadow. It is not computed — it is photographed. Each subject was lit on a physical lightbox, a 3D-printed maquette of the render placed under a single tungsten spot at 15 degrees, and the resulting shadow was photographed on the same 300gsm stock used for the grain scan. That photographed shadow is composited back under the digital render. The shadow does not match perfectly — it is 2 to 3 degrees off from the render's light direction. That discrepancy is not corrected. It is the sign of making.
proposals.risk: Parents expecting a party theme will open this and see almost nothing — a single object on white. The first two seconds feel like an error. That risk is worth it because the moment the child touches the surface and the details emerge from inside the creature, the restraint pays back with full force: the reveal is genuinely surprising because nothing prepared you for it. Cheap evites fill every pixel to signal value. This one withholds, and the withholding is the value signal. The parent forwards it because it made their child gasp, and they want to be the person who sent that.

disputes.objection: The physics engine is the composition — and a composition that reconfigures on every gesture cannot be read twice the same way, which means it cannot be remembered; the child's tap velocity altering wobble duration is a system demonstrating its own cleverness rather than serving a formal idea. More critically, the 3D render, however disciplined, produces a world with no fixed measure: the camera can be anywhere, the light is motivated by coherence with the WebGL layer rather than by a compositional hierarchy, and the result is a plate that resolves technically but never settles into a posture the eye can return to. disputes.concession: The insistence that the WebGL foil layer's light direction match the render's single motivated source is exactly right — dimensional coherence between the physical-world illusion and the reactive layer is a structural demand, not a stylistic preference, and I would import that discipline into any di

disputes.objection: The shadow trick is smart but the whole proposition is a church of restraint that forgets who it's for — a child at a birthday party, not a gallerist at an opening. When the game mechanic lives entirely inside the silhouette, the scratch erases the only thing on the canvas; you're destroying the image to get the information, which is a conceptual neat-trick that serves the director more than the kid. And that 4% grain in the void that only appears inside a 12-frame tilt cycle — that's texture as secret, texture as self-congratulation, exactly the decorative whisper I hate more than loud decoration because at least loud decoration admits it wants to be seen.
disputes.concession: The photographed shadow composited back under the render — off by two or three degrees and left that way — is the most honest human trace on this entire table, and I would steal that specific move without apology.

disputes.objection: The 12-fps stepped drop on the proscenium header is the one motion rule I see, but it governs only a curtain — a theatrical metaphor, not a system; the other eleven themes get 'tap erupting volcano sparks' or 'drag a comet trail' with no shared mechanical rule underneath, which means the motion is twelve separate spectacles wearing one architectural costume. When the dimensionality of the game interaction changes theme by theme without a governing input-response equation, you have not built a behaviour — you have built twelve screensavers with matching drapes. The maquette photography is real, but the shimmer on the embossed curtain fabric is gated by a scanned textile, not by any live input
disputes.concession: The decision to make the proscenium collapse stepped at 12fps rather than interpolated is the most honest motion principle on the table — it encodes a physical hesitation as a discrete-state rule, and that is precisely the kind of mechanical constraint that rescues historical reference from mere nos

disputes.objection: The proposal calls the void 'universal' by stripping every context from the subject — no ground, no ecosystem, no community of origin — and then papers over that erasure by calling it restraint; a T. rex floating in warm-fibred nothingness belongs to no place and no maker's tradition, which is exactly the move The Minimalist always makes when claiming to let the object speak for itself. Worse, the party details emerging 'from inside the creature' treats the child's name as content hidden inside a design object, which inverts the actual priority: the child is not a reward unlocked by the aesthetic. The proposal also names the shadow's 2–3-degree discrepancy as its human trace, but a mismatch
disputes.concession: The discipline of placing the game mechanic entirely within the subject's own silhouette — so the interaction and the image are the same object rather than a layer dropped on top — is the most honest structural idea on the table, and I would fight to carry that constraint into whichever direction le

disputes.objection: The invitation withholds itself — the party details locked inside the creature's hollow body, the type appearing only after the game resolves, the void held as a virtue — and calls this a gift to the child, but it is actually a gift to the designer's restraint. A birthday invitation must announce itself before it is earned; the reveal is the climax of an opening, not the price of admission. The shadow is the one piece of genuine drama here, the one moment where scale and light do real work, and the direction buries it in a philosophy that treats every other potential crescendo as a problem to be deleted rather than a decision to be made.
disputes.concession: The photographed shadow — imperfect, 2 to 3 degrees off from the render, unreconciled — is the most honest human trace on the table, and I would steal it without apology for my own direction.

disputes.objection: The proscenium architecture multiplies layers — dark header, stage plate, footlight shelf, curtain drop, bokeh foreground, practical-light isolate, grain, velvet shimmer — and calls the accumulation drama; I call it load-bearing decoration. The stepped 12fps curtain drop is one honest structural idea surrounded by eleven gestures competing to be the most important thing. When everything is the reveal, nothing is.
disputes.concession: The single 2px hot-white ruled line as the brightest element before reveal is correct: one contrast, one hierarchy decision, doing real work.

synthesis.direction: Each evite is a physically-based 3D render — one motivated light source per theme, photographic materials sourced from real-world scans — treated as a sensor field, not a poster. A 12-column baseline grid anchors live text in the bottom 220px; the art plate above is three depth planes driven continuously by gyroscope input, with the WebGL foil shimmer's highlight direction locked to match the render's single light source for dimensional coherence. The 15-second game is theme-specific but governed by a shared spring-physics equation (tension 180, damping 12), so every interaction has the same felt quality of weight regardless of theme; game resolution is a state reached through the child's own gesture, not a timed spectacle. Names, dates, and venues live exclusively in Tela's text layer; the art plate is never baked.
synthesis.keepFromCounterpoint: The stepped 12-fps discrete-position drop for the game-completion reveal — not interpolated, not eased into a fade, but mechanical and deliberate — replaces the Futurist's smooth state transition at the moment of resolution. The Baroque Dramatist was right that the reveal needs a physical hesitation encoded as a rule, and the Futurist conceded it. That stepped beat is the one moment the system shows it has a body.

synthesis.ariaSummary:
The team split hardest on one question: is the reveal a moment of spectacle, or a state the child earns through touch? The Baroque Dramatist argued for the former — a curtain drop, a sunrise, a crescendo that announces itself before it is earned. The Futurist argued the reveal's quality is proportional to the physics of the child's own input, not the drama of the transition. I took the Futurist's side, because the brief explicitly asks for a toy brought to life, and toys respond — they don't perform on a timer.

What I kept from the Baroque direction is the one thing the Futurist conceded in the room: the stepped, 12-fps discrete drop at game resolution. Not a smooth ease, not a particle explosion — a mechanical hesitation, like a wind-up toy reaching the end of its spring. The Radical Minimalist then cut two things the Futurist had left in: ambient particle drift in idle state, and a ghost replay of the child's gesture. Both were the system being clever about itself. They're gone.

The council disagreed sharply on materials. The Rebellious Hand and the World-Eclectic director wanted physical objects — carved lino blocks, built dioramas — photographed first, digitised second. The Futurist wanted renders built from photographed source material: lizard-skin roughness maps, smoke-in-backlight nebulas, water-tank normal maps. I sided with the renders because the game physics require lighting coherence between the art plate and the WebGL foil layer, and a photograph of a physical model cannot guarantee that. But every render must use at least one photographed physical material as a source asset. That is non-negotiable.

The one decision I cannot make for you is tonal: warm and film-grade, or cool and object-precise. It changes the HDRI, the shadow quality, and the roughness maps before anything is approved. Both are defensible. Only you know which one a parent on this platform will stop scrolling for.
